sections.heading: What are Binary Search Tree Patterns?
sections.content: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree where, for every node, all values in the left subtree are smaller and all values in the right subtree are larger. This ordering lets you discard half of the tree at each step, like binary search, so search, insert and delete take O(h) time, where h is the height. In a balanced tree h is about log n. BST problems either use this property to prune the search or use the fact that an inorder traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order.

sections.heading: Balanced vs Skewed
sections.content: Inserting sorted data into a plain BST produces a chain, which behaves like a linked list. Self-balancing trees (AVL and Red-Black trees) rotate nodes to keep the height near log n. In Kotlin you rarely build one yourself, because TreeMap and TreeSet are red-black trees and give O(log n) operations with floor, ceiling, first and last helpers.

Need elements in sorted order or by rank: inorder traversal, stop early when possible

Using TreeMap and TreeSet Instead of a Hand-Built BST
sections.code:
import java.util.TreeMap
import java.util.TreeSet

val set = TreeSet<Int>()
set.add(10); set.add(20); set.add(30)
set.first()               // 10   smallest
set.last()                // 30   largest
set.floor(25)             // 20   largest <= 25
set.ceiling(25)           // 30   smallest >= 25
set.lower(20)             // 10   largest < 20
set.higher(20)            // 30   smallest > 20
set.headSet(20)           // elements < 20
set.tailSet(20)           // elements >= 20
set.subSet(10, 30)        // elements in [10, 30)

val map = TreeMap<Int, String>()
map[5] = "a"
map.floorKey(7)           // 5
map.ceilingKey(7)         // null if nothing is >= 7
map.firstEntry()
map.pollFirstEntry()      // remove and return the smallest
// Every operation: O(log n)

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Validating a BST by comparing only with the parent, which misses violations deeper in the tree
Using Int bounds with Int.MIN_VALUE or Int.MAX_VALUE as node values (use Long or nullable bounds)
Treating equal values inconsistently: decide whether duplicates go left, right or are disallowed
Forgetting to reconnect the child pointer after a recursive insert or delete
Deleting a two-child node without handling the successor's own removal
Doing a full O(n) traversal when the BST property allows an O(h) path
Assuming O(log n) without noting that a skewed tree gives O(n)
Using a plain list or sorted array when TreeMap or TreeSet would give O(log n) updates

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: In a BST, left values are smaller and right values are larger for every node
That ordering lets you search, insert and delete in O(h) by discarding one subtree each step
Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted, which solves kth smallest, validation and neighbor-difference problems
Validate with ancestor ranges, not only with the parent
Deleting a node with two children copies the inorder successor and removes it from the right subtree
A sorted array becomes a balanced BST by choosing the middle as the root, and TreeMap or TreeSet give a ready-made balanced tree
